articles.title: Tariffs Continue to Condition Markets as Companies React to Corporate Accounts
articles.summary: The current earnings season is being impacted by commercial tariffs implemented by the US and the financial reports of large corporations. According to Generali Investments, 'we cannot yet estimate the damage that tariffs will cause to global growth.' In contrast, the German government's announcement of a new fiscal plan and a defense investment package has boosted European markets, particularly in Frankfurt. However, the situation is different in the US, where the first three months were marked by high instability due to the application of tariffs, raising concerns that the US economy may enter recession. The data indicates a negative growth of 0.3% in the US economy during the first quarter, with a 6% increase in earnings per share, which is lower than the numbers achieved in the fourth quarter of 2024 and a disappointment compared to the initial growth expectation of 11%.

articles.title: Trump's Trade War Uncertainty: US Stocks Rise Amid Tariff Concerns
articles.summary: The US stock market closed high on Tuesday, with the S&P 500 index and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rising for the sixth consecutive day. US President Trump signed an executive order to avoid additional tariffs on the automotive industry, and US Commerce Secretary Lighthizer revealed that a trade agreement has been reached with a certain country, which has boosted investor confidence in the trade war. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 300.03 points, or 0.8%, to 40,527.62; the S&P 500 index rose 32.08 points, or 0.6%, to 5,560.83; and the Nasdaq Composite Index rose 95.19 points, or 0.6%, to 17,461.32. Despite the S&P 500 index rising 8% in the past six days, it still shows the largest decline in the first 100 days of a new president's term since 1973, under President Nixon. US Treasury yields fell, with the 10-year Treasury yield falling to 4.171%, down from 4.21% on Monday. US Treasury Secretary Mnuchin predicted that China may lose 1 million jobs due to tariffs, but also hinted that trade agreements have been made with Japan and India. Trump signed an executive order on Tuesday before the close, providing a tax credit of up to 15% of the domestic value of assembled vehicles. This tax credit can be used to offset the value of imported parts, giving automakers time to transfer their supply chain back to the US. Automakers responded little to this news. General Motors (GM) fell 0.6%, the company withdrew its 2025 profit guidance and suspended a $40 billion stock buyback plan due to tariff impacts. The US trade deficit in goods expanded to a record high in March, with companies importing heavily before Trump's tariffs took effect. The Conference Board reported that the US Consumer Confidence Index fell to its lowest level since May 2020, while job openings showed a relatively stable labor market. Raymond James investment strategist Larry Adam said, 'We've passed the biggest uncertainty of tariffs, but I think we're getting closer to the peak of economic uncertainty.' Amazon (AMZN) fell initially, but later narrowed its decline after the White House press secretary called the company's plan to show the impact of tariffs on product prices 'hostile'; Amazon later denied plans to display the tariff costs, and its stock price subsequently narrowed its decline, closing down 0.2%. UPS (UPS) fell 0.4%, the company expects to lay off 200,000 people and close some facilities this year. Honeywell (HON) reported a 5.4% increase in adjusted earnings, and its stock price surged 5.4% at close. Sherwin-Williams (SHW) also reported a 4.8% increase in earnings, which boosted the Dow Jones Industrial Average. Coca-Cola (KO) reported revenue and earnings that exceeded expectations, and its stock price rose 0.8%. More economic data will be released this week, including the government's employment report on Friday, as well as Apple and Microsoft's earnings reports. Investors remain concerned about the impact of tariffs.

articles.title: US PMI Data Tonight: Will it Reveal a Recession?
articles.summary: As the tariff storm disrupts the US economy, concerns about economic slowdown have been weighing on the market. Tonight's PMI data may reveal whether the US is in a recession or not, and weak data will further hit US stocks and the US dollar. According to Bloomberg's survey, the Markit PMI index for April is expected to drop to 52.2, lower than the 53.5 in March. The initial value of the manufacturing PMI is expected to fall to 49, back into the contraction zone. The input price index in the US manufacturing PMI is particularly worth watching, as it rose to its fastest pace in nearly two years in March, reflecting increased pressure on business costs. Analysts predict that under the pressure of tariffs, the April data will continue to rise. Additionally, a decline in new orders may indicate a broad economic contraction, and the employment sub-index will reflect the willingness of enterprises to recruit. In the midst of market turmoil and tariff uncertainty, the performance of today's PMI data is particularly important. A series of weak PMI data will increase the risk of further declines in US stocks and the US dollar, exacerbating negative sentiment in the market. Analysts say that if the PMI is more pessimistic than expected, US stocks will face even greater selling pressure. If market attention to PMI indices decreases, they will likely focus on the ISM index to be released in early May. In the current context where the independence of the Federal Reserve is under threat, weak PMI and ISM manufacturing data will put more pressure on the US dollar. When the US PMI performs worse than other developed countries' PMI (as is the case now), it usually leads to a weakening of the US dollar.

articles.title: Tariff turmoil prompts cloudy forecasts from U.S. companies for year ahead: report
articles.summary: The latest round of financial results and forecasts for U.S. companies is uncertain due to the impact of tariffs and a shift in U.S. policy, reported The Associated Press. The U.S. economy shrank in the first quarter, and consumer spending has increased, possibly to get ahead of tariffs. Companies are pulling back on hiring, and roughly half of the S&P 500 companies have reported their quarterly financial results, focusing on adjusting to tariffs and changing consumer behavior. The situation remains unpredictable due to President Donald Trump's on-again-off-again policy, making it difficult for companies to plan ahead and investors to seek stability. According to the report, 'stunted consumer spending and weaker employment could further hurt the U.S. economy,' and 'the situation remains unpredictable and that is problematic for companies trying to plan ahead and investors looking for stability.'
